transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Well, honestly, I wasn't going to come in, but... something's been happening at work that really scared me. I work as a surveillance officer, so I spend a lot of time in a quiet room looking at monitors. Lately, during the really quiet stretches, I've been hearing voices coming through the monitor speakers. 

They say things like, "You missed it, Ruth," or... "People are going to get hurt because of you." The thing is, I know every channel is muted. And when my coworkers are in the room, they don't hear a thing. It's just me.
Before you started hearing these voices at work, had you been experiencing any periods of feeling unusually depressed, hopeless, or very elevated and energetic in mood?

No, not really. I mean, I've been feeling pretty down lately, but that only started after they changed the surveillance lead at work. Since then, I've just felt... really hopeless, and guilty all the time, like I'm doing everything wrong. 

But before this specific low period, no. I've never felt like this, and I definitely never heard voices accusing me through the equipment before. I also never felt so... sure that I was a danger to everyone around me. It seems like the voices and those awful beliefs only started happening since I've been feeling so depressed.
Before this current period of feeling down and hopeless that started after the change at work, have you ever had other times in your life when you felt depressed or hopeless for a week or longer?

No, I haven't. I mean, everyone has bad days, but... nothing like this. I've never felt this kind of deep, constant hopelessness before, not for a week or longer. This is the first time it's ever gotten this bad.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F33.3 (recurrent depressive disorder) because patient denies any prior episodes of depression lasting a week or longer. This is her first major depressive episode. The psychotic features (auditory hallucinations and delusions of guilt/harm) are clearly secondary to the current depressive episode, supporting F32.3 (major depressive disorder, single episode, with psychotic features) rather than a primary psychotic disorder.

The depressive symptoms (hopelessness, guilt, feeling like a failure) preceded and appear to be the primary driver of the psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations with depressive content, delusion of being a danger). The psychotic symptoms are mood-congruent and emerged in the context of a clear depressive episode triggered by a specific workplace stressor. No prior history of mood episodes or psychotic symptoms. The depressive episode is the primary diagnosis with psychotic features as a specifier.
